result:
There's a particular quality to the light in late afternoon, in autumn especially, that seems to carry some kind of message I've never quite been able to decode. It slants in low and gold and makes ordinary things—a chipped coffee mug, a stack of mail, the dust suspended in air—look like they're being asked a question. I don't know what the question is. Maybe it's just: did you notice me? Did you notice any of this while it was happening?

I think a lot about attention lately. Not in the productivity-guru sense, not as a resource to be optimized or protected from the algorithmic hordes, but as something closer to love. To attend to something is to love it a little, even if it's just a glass of water or the particular way your neighbor's dog favors his left front paw when he walks. The philosopher Simone Weil said attention was the rarest and purest form of generosity. I believe her, though I rarely manage it myself. My mind is a dog off its leash, running toward every rabbit, every shiny thing, every old grievance buried in the yard.

There's a kind of writing you do when you're trying to say something, and a kind you do when you're trying to find out if there's anything to say. This is the second kind. I don't know where it's going. That's either honest or lazy, and maybe those aren't as different as we pretend.

I keep thinking about how strange it is that we agree on words. That "tree" means tree to you and to me, more or less, despite the fact that you're picturing a different tree than I am, from a different childhood, a different climate, different light. Language is this enormous shared hallucination we've all agreed to have together, and it mostly works, which still strikes me as something close to a miracle. Or at least an enormous stroke of luck. Babel should have worked. The fact that it didn't—that we can still, mostly, talk to each other—feels worth pausing on.

I had a thought yesterday about rivers, how they don't really have a self in the way we imagine selves. A river is just water passing through a shape. The shape persists, more or less, while the water that constitutes it at any given moment is already gone, already become something else—ocean, cloud, rain on someone else's roof. Maybe that's closer to what a person is, too. Not a fixed thing but a shape that water keeps passing through. The cells replace themselves. The opinions replace themselves, if you're lucky, if you're paying attention (there's that word again). What persists is some pattern, some particular bend in the riverbed, some way of turning toward or away from the light.

I'm aware this is the kind of thing that sounds profound at eleven at night and slightly embarrassing by morning. I'm writing it anyway because that's the assignment, more or less. Whatever comes. Not whatever survives editing, not whatever would make a good essay, just whatever surfaces when you stop trying to direct the surfacing.

Here's something that surfaced: I miss handwriting letters. Actual letters, on paper, that took days to arrive and contained news that was already slightly old by the time you read it. There was something honest about that lag. You knew, reading it, that the person who wrote "I am happy today" might not be happy anymore, might have already moved through three other moods by the time you found out about the first one. It built a kind of humility into communication. Now everything arrives instantly and we've started to expect instant responses too, as if feeling were a service with an SLA. I don't think this has made us happier. I don't think it's made us worse either, necessarily—it's just changed the texture of things, the way a fabric changes when you switch from wool to something synthetic. Still keeps you warm. Doesn't breathe the same.

I wonder sometimes what people two hundred years from now will think was obviously, embarrassingly wrong about how we lived. Every generation has this blind spot, this thing future people will shake their heads about—the way we shake our heads about bloodletting or the divine right of kings or the casual cruelty toward people who loved differently. I have guesses but I distrust my guesses, because if I could actually see the blind spot clearly it wouldn't be blind anymore. That's the nature of the thing. It's not that the answer is hidden; it's that the question hasn't been asked yet, or has been asked only by a few people everyone else considers cranks.

Maybe that's worth remembering when you meet a crank. Not all of them are right, obviously—most cranks are just wrong, loudly, with great confidence. But some small percentage of them are early, not wrong, just early, standing in the wrong century making a true claim that doesn't have a home yet. I don't know how you tell the difference in real time. I suspect you mostly can't. I suspect history sorts it out for you, unhelpfully, after everyone involved is dead.

The light's changed since I started writing this. It's not gold anymore, just gray, the ordinary gray of a sky deciding to become evening. The mug is still chipped. The mail is still unsorted. Nothing got resolved, no real argument got made, no thesis got proven. But something got noticed, which I suppose was the whole quiet point of doing this at all—not to arrive anywhere, just to see what happens when you let your attention drift along its own bent riverbed for a while, trusting that the shape, whatever it is, was worth following even without knowing in advance where it would empty out.
